XIAOXUAN SHEN, FENGHUA YU, and QIAN WAN, National Engineering Research Center
of Educational Big Data, Central China Normal University, Wuhan, China and Faculty of Artificial
Intelligence in Education, Central China Normal University, Wuhan, China

Knowledge Tracing (KT) is the task of predicting students’ future performance based on their past interactions
with educational resources. A key aspect of KT is representation learning, which aims to capture meaningful
features from students’ learning behaviors to improve prediction performance. Recently, contrastive learning
methods have shown great promise in representation learning. As a result, KT models based on contrastive
learning have been introduced to enhance representation learning for KT. However, these models have posed
several challenges. Firstly, most of these models adopt the contrastive learning approach used in other fields,
which involves data augmentation followed by contrastive learning, yet efectively applying data augmentation
in KT remains an open challenge. Secondly, these models typically apply contrastive learning to only one
of the fundamental components of KT: questions, interactions, or knowledge states, thereby limiting their
overall performance. To address these issues, this article proposes a Multi-level Contrastive learning model
for Knowledge Tracing (MCKT). MCKT (The code can be found at https://github.com/lilstrawberry/MCKT.)
does not rely on data augmentation strategies; instead, it deeply integrates domain knowledge and performs
contrastive learning at three levels: questions, interactions, and knowledge states. Experimental results on
four publicly available datasets, compared against a total of 20 state-of-the-art KT models, demonstrate that
MCKT consistently outperforms other models. Subsequent experiments further validate the efectiveness of
the multi-level contrastive learning approach.

1 Introduction
In recent years, with the rapid development of multimedia technology, educational methods have
become increasingly diverse. Particularly since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, online
education using the internet as a medium has gained widespread popularity. Online education
platforms such as MOOCs and Coursera have atracted a large number of learners. As online
education data accumulates, mining the underlying learning paterns is of paramount importance
[77]. Once these learning paterns are captured, educators can tailor instruction to address learners’
weaknesses, continually improving their abilities, thus achieving a more personalized form of
education [56]. Knowledge Tracing (KT) plays a crucial role in online education systems, pre-
dicting students’ future performance based on their past interactions with educational resources.
Efectively addressing KT tasks undoubtedly assists educators in beter understanding students’
learning needs, thereby providing more personalized and targeted educational support [3].
A simple illustration of KT is shown in Figure 1. In this illustration, each question contains one
or more relevant concepts, and students practice with diferent questions. Their knowledge state,
which represents their mastery of knowledge, constantly evolves as they progress. KT involves
predicting students’ future performance when answering questions. A key element in achieving
accurate predictions is efective representation learning, which captures meaningful features from
students’ learning behaviors and provides a foundation for modeling the dynamic progression
of their knowledge over time. Clearly, how to trace and represent students’ knowledge states is
crucial for KT [1, 43, 47]. In addition, in KT, the number of questions is often very high, leading to
sparse interaction data between students and questions [6] (interaction here refers to students’
responses to questions in KT, typically indicating whether a question was answered correctly

2 Related Work
In this section, we first review the fundamental work of KT. Then, we explore two topics relevant
to this article: Representation learning for KT and contrastive learning for KT.
2.1 KT
KT can be traced back to the proposal of Bayesian KT [11]. In subsequent work, there have
also been some KT methods based on factor analysis introduced [5, 42, 65, 69]. In this article,
we focus exclusively on deep learning-based KT models. In recent years, with the rise of deep
learning techniques, research in KT based on deep learning has made significant advancements.
We categorize KT models into the following four types based on their characteristics: Sequential
based, Memory based, Graph based, and Atention based.
Sequential Based. In sequential-based KT modeling methods, DKT [43] was the first deep learning-
based KT model to use LSTM [23] to trace students’ knowledge states and achieved impressive
performance. Considering that DKT cannot reconstruct observed inputs and has unstable knowl-
edge states, DKT+ [76] proposed to enhance DKT by introducing reconstruction error and stable
knowledge states. As knowledge forgeting is inevitable during the student learning process,
DKT+forgeting [38] incorporated forgeting mechanisms into DKT to enhance its performance.
ATKT [19] found that deep learning-based KT models have a risk of overfiting and introduced
adversarial training [17] to mitigate overfiting. LPKT [46] focuses on maintaining the consistency
of students’ knowledge states during their learning process, enhancing interpretability while main-
taining high performance. DIMKT [45] delves into the impact of question dificulty on students’
knowledge states to enhance KT. LBKT [73] explores the influence of students’ learning behavior
and knowledge states in-depth to strengthen KT.
Memory Based. In memory-based KT modeling methods, DKVMN [79] was the first to propose a
Dynamic Key-Value Memory Network to model students’ knowledge states, considering that each
concept is associated with many potential knowledge concepts. SKVMN [1], based on DKVMN,
introduced a Hop-LSTM structure to enhance the representation capability of knowledge states.
DGMN [2] considers relationships between latent concepts and takes into account students’
forgeting behaviors. MAN [22] addresses skill transition phenomena and proposes a memory-
enhanced atention network.
Graph Based. In graph-based KT modeling methods, GKT [39] designed multiple strategies
to construct knowledge graph structures and propagated knowledge states on this graph. SKT
[63] considered various relationships between concepts on the graph, such as prerequisite and
similarity relationships. HGKT [62] proposes a hierarchical graph KT to explore potentially complex
relationships between exercises.
Atention Based. In atention-based KT modeling methods, SAKT [40] was the first to use a
self-atention mechanism to capture the degree of student atention to concepts in building their
knowledge states. SAINT [9] used a Transformer [64] to construct students’ knowledge states. AKT
[16] proposes a context-aware atention architecture to simulate students’ forgeting behavior.
sparseKT [24] recognizes the risk of overfiting on small datasets in KT and introduces a sparse
atention KT model to enhance KT robustness.

2.1 KT
KT can be traced back to the proposal of Bayesian KT [11]. In subsequent work, there have
also been some KT methods based on factor analysis introduced [5, 42, 65, 69]. In this article,
we focus exclusively on deep learning-based KT models. In recent years, with the rise of deep
learning techniques, research in KT based on deep learning has made significant advancements.
We categorize KT models into the following four types based on their characteristics: Sequential
based, Memory based, Graph based, and Atention based.
Sequential Based. In sequential-based KT modeling methods, DKT [43] was the first deep learning-
based KT model to use LSTM [23] to trace students’ knowledge states and achieved impressive
performance. Considering that DKT cannot reconstruct observed inputs and has unstable knowl-
edge states, DKT+ [76] proposed to enhance DKT by introducing reconstruction error and stable
knowledge states. As knowledge forgeting is inevitable during the student learning process,
DKT+forgeting [38] incorporated forgeting mechanisms into DKT to enhance its performance.
ATKT [19] found that deep learning-based KT models have a risk of overfiting and introduced
adversarial training [17] to mitigate overfiting. LPKT [46] focuses on maintaining the consistency
of students’ knowledge states during their learning process, enhancing interpretability while main-
taining high performance. DIMKT [45] delves into the impact of question dificulty on students’
knowledge states to enhance KT. LBKT [73] explores the influence of students’ learning behavior
and knowledge states in-depth to strengthen KT.
Memory Based. In memory-based KT modeling methods, DKVMN [79] was the first to propose a
Dynamic Key-Value Memory Network to model students’ knowledge states, considering that each
concept is associated with many potential knowledge concepts. SKVMN [1], based on DKVMN,
introduced a Hop-LSTM structure to enhance the representation capability of knowledge states.
DGMN [2] considers relationships between latent concepts and takes into account students’
forgeting behaviors. MAN [22] addresses skill transition phenomena and proposes a memory-
enhanced atention network.
Graph Based. In graph-based KT modeling methods, GKT [39] designed multiple strategies
to construct knowledge graph structures and propagated knowledge states on this graph. SKT
[63] considered various relationships between concepts on the graph, such as prerequisite and
similarity relationships. HGKT [62] proposes a hierarchical graph KT to explore potentially complex
relationships between exercises.
Atention Based. In atention-based KT modeling methods, SAKT [40] was the first to use a
self-atention mechanism to capture the degree of student atention to concepts in building their
knowledge states. SAINT [9] used a Transformer [64] to construct students’ knowledge states. AKT
[16] proposes a context-aware atention architecture to simulate students’ forgeting behavior.
sparseKT [24] recognizes the risk of overfiting on small datasets in KT and introduces a sparse
atention KT model to enhance KT robustness.

processes, KT consists of three fundamental components: questions, interactions, and knowledge
Questions. Questions refer to the exercises or learning units that students encounter during
their learning process. They form the most fundamental component of KT. To enhance question
representations, researchers have made numerous eforts: DHKT [66] explores the relationships
between questions to constrain their representations. EERNN [53] leverages textual information of
questions, using word2vec [37] to obtain question embeddings. AKT [16], inspired by the Rasch
[44] model, positions question representations near relevant concepts. MIKT [58] extends AKT by
introducing an extended Rasch model, accommodating multi-concept representations for questions.

Knowledge States. Knowledge states represent a student’s implicit mastery of knowledge concepts,
making them the core of predicting future performance. Numerous approaches have been proposed
to model and represent knowledge states efectively: DKT [43] employs LSTMs to trace students’

knowledge state representations. LBKT [73] incorporates multiple learning behaviors to enhance the
representation of knowledge states. ReKT [47] adopts a multi-perspective approach for representing
student knowledge states. GRKT [13] applies Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the
interdependencies among concepts for more accurate knowledge state representations.
In summary, questions, interactions, and knowledge states are the foundational components of
KT. Efectively representing them is critical to advancing KT models and improving their predictive
performance.
2.3 Contrastive Learning for KT
Contrastive learning is a specialized branch of self-supervised learning [32]. In recent years,
contrastive learning has demonstrated strong representation learning capabilities in various fields
such as computer vision [8, 18, 20], natural language processing [15, 72], GNNs [61, 78, 82], and
more. These studies indicate that customized data augmentation strategies tailored to specific tasks
are crucial for the success of contrastive learning. Various data augmentation strategies, such as
cropping and rotation for images in computer vision, synonym replacement and word insertion for
natural language processing, and feature masking and random edge removal for GNNs, have been
shown to be efective.
The KT methods based on contrastive learning are still in their early stages, with only a limited
amount of research using contrastive learning methods to promote KT. Bi-CLKT [51] was the first
to introduce contrastive learning into KT, using it on both question-question graphs and concept-
concept graphs, following the paradigm of graph augmentation-contrastive learning, to obtain
representations of questions and concepts. TCL4KT [54] represents questions from three diferent
perspectives on the concept-question-student heterogeneous graph to perform contrastive learning
and enhance DKT.

Unlike these contrastive learning-based KT methods, there are several key diferences with
MCKT. Firstly, MCKT’s contrastive learning does not rely on data augmentation strategies, whereas
they all require designing various data augmentation strategies for contrastive learning. Although
combining contrastive learning has been proven efective in these methods, the impact it brings
remains unknown. For example, in methods like CL4KT and DTransformer, they involve random
swapping of students’ answer sequences and flipping the correctness of student responses. While
these approaches align with intuition, their efects on students’ experience and learning in real
educational setings are still unknown. Secondly, they all focus solely on modeling one of the
three fundamental elements of KT: the question, interaction, or knowledge state, disregarding
the crucial role of other elements. While methods like TCL4KT [54] represent questions from
various perspectives, it still primarily constructs contrastive learning at the question-level. In
contrast, MCKT constructs multi-level contrastive learning, encompassing the question-level,
interaction-level, and knowledge state-level.
It is worth noting that MCKT can further enhance its performance by integrating graph structures.
Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) [4, 68] can capture complex relationships among questions,
interactions, and knowledge states by modeling them as graph nodes. Through graph atention
mechanisms or other techniques, GCL can focus on relevant connections, improving MCKT’s ability
to learn contextual and semantic relationships. This integration will boost MCKT’s representation
learning and performance in modeling student knowledge. We leave this aspect for future work.

6 Application
One of the most interesting applications of KT is probably monitoring students’ knowledge states.
Once a student’s knowledge state is accurately captured, teachers can provide targeted guidance
to address their weaknesses in understanding. In this section, we randomly selected a student’s
answer records for five questions over 25 timesteps from the ASSIST09 dataset and visualized the
student’s knowledge state for each question at each timestep.
As shown in Figure 9(a), the y-axis represents the questions that the student answered, with
diferent questions distinguished by diferent colored circles. The x-axis represents the student’s
interactions (questions and responses), with correct answers shown as the corresponding circles
and incorrect answers having an additional white circle. Each element in the matrix represents
the student’s mastery of the question at that moment, with larger values indicating a beter
understanding. We can draw the following conclusions: (1) When a student answers a question
correctly/incorrectly, their mastery of that question significantly increases/decreases, which aligns
with intuition because correctness in answering questions does reflect a student’s knowledge level

questions significantly improves from the first timestep to the last timestep, even if the student

their knowledge mastery.

7 Conclusions and Future Work
In this article, we propose a novel Multi-level Contrastive learning for Knowledge Tracing (MCKT).
Unlike relying on data augmentation strategies, MCKT delves deep into domain knowledge and
leverages contrastive learning at three distinct levels to acquire representations conducive to KT:
question-level, interaction-level, and knowledge state-level. Furthermore, we model student learning
data from diferent perspectives to comprehensively capture their knowledge state. Extensive
experiments on four publicly available datasets demonstrate that MCKT outperforms other KT
models significantly. Ablation experiments confirm the efectiveness of multi-level contrastive
learning.
Of course, MCKT still ofers room for further improvements. The way question-level and
interaction-level contrastive learning selects positive samples relies on the concept labels be-
hind the questions. While using concept labels in questions is a prevalent practice in current KT
models, exploring methods to overcome this limitation is a promising direction. Additionally,
MCKT lacks interpretability, although this is a common issue in most KT models, a more decision-
transparent KT model would certainly be more desirable. Lastly, the complex relationships between
questions, interactions, and knowledge states can be further explored using graph structures to
more efectively capture the semantic connections between them. In future work, we will investigate
how to address MCKT’s reliance on concept labels using unsupervised methods. Simultaneously,
we will introduce additional interpretable components to enhance the interpretability of MCKT,
such as atention scores and IRT predictions. Furthermore, we plan to apply GCL to delve deeper
into the complex relationships between questions, interactions, and knowledge states by model-
ing them as graph nodes. By leveraging methods like graph atention networks, we aim to learn
the dependencies between them and further uncover the relationships between questions and
interactions, questions and knowledge states, as well as interactions and knowledge states. This
will improve MCKT’s ability to model contextual information and semantic connections, thereby
enhancing its overall performance.
